hook: A print shop owner has one big press and one Saturday. A wedding couple wants invitations, a store wants banners, a cafe wants menus. She can print only one job, so taking one means turning down the others. Every person, business and government faces the same squeeze: there is never enough to do everything, so every choice gives something up.

prereq.why: Compare the values directly: 900 is the largest.

prereq.why: The horizontal axis runs along the bottom.

figure.caption: Unlimited wants and limited resources make scarcity, so every choice has a trade-off. Maya picks a \$96 lifeguard shift; its opportunity cost is the next-best choice, \$60 of tutoring, not \$100. Invented example.

ideas: Scarcity: limited resources and unlimited wants. It affects rich and poor people, firms and governments alike.

The factors of production (resources) are land (natural resources), labor (human effort), capital (tools, machines, buildings) and entrepreneurship (organizing and risk taking). Money is not capital in this sense.
Most resources are scarce, but some are not used up when used: an idea or a piece of knowledge can be shared by everyone at once.
Every choice is a trade-off. Its opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative given up: one option, not all of them added together.

misconception.wrong: The opportunity cost of Maya's lifeguard shift is \$100: the \$60 of tutoring plus the \$40 of soccer she gave up.
misconception.right: She could have done only one of the other two, so the opportunity cost is the single next-best choice: tutoring, worth \$60.

summary: Scarcity means resources are limited while wants are not, so every choice involves a trade-off. The resources used to make goods and services are the factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship. The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next-best alternative you give up, only the next best, and it includes time and other things that are not paid for in money.
